With Covid rampant right now, as well as food prices going up significantly this year (at least in Northern California) lots of us have resorted to supplementing our own food supply via growing our own. Less time in public=safest option. It's nice to not have to go to the grocery store as often for fresh produce, and it's hard to beat the flavor of organically grown crops that aren't sprayed with crazy chemicals that shrink your you know what! Your brain of course! Sheesh.

Growing your own food on a significant scale, especially around here, comes with challenges: squirrels, gophers, voles, moles, raccoons, rabbits, deer, rats, mice, and in my case pill bugs! Yes, who would have thought pill bugs would DEVASTATE all of my root crops which are directly sown in the ground?! In order to succeed, we have to grow starts and transplant in pots before planting them in the ground. Anything that goes directly in the ground gets eaten before it has a chance to grow! For this reason, we can't grow root crops here until an organic solution to the pill bug situation is figured out. Maybe we'll solarize the soil in the summer (cover with black plastic and cook everything that way)


Enough talk, let's peep out the photos!



Asian Greens that have names I can't pronounce:



OMG, if you're making soup, this stuff is amazing! Drop the leaves in there for 30 seconds or so, just enough to wilt and BAM! Amazing texture and flavor. This is like a smaller version of Napa Cabbage, but with way more succulent, crunchier leaves. It's for sure a unique selection (package said it's a Taiwanese cultivar and a bunch of stuff in chinese that I can't read). Organically grown, this stuff actually has some depth of flavor:


No clue what this is, never seen it at asian markets. It's some sort of mustard green:


This is commonly known as chinese broccoli aka Chinese Kale aka Kai-lan(spelling?) I always hear my wife call it "Guy-LAAAAN," she speaks Cantonese, so for those of you who speak chinglish, you'll know what a homie is talking about:



And here's Celery! Have you ever tried starting it from seeds? They grow just slightly faster than Sarracenia, LOL These are 2 months old.....2 MONTHS!!!! They'll probably start growing much faster once they reach a certain size. This is my prized crop, have you ever tasted home grown celery? You'll become a food a-hole once you see how delicious it is home-grown:



Let's see what kind of veggies you have going in your garden? feel free to post pics and stories here!

posts.body_html:
Your greens look so nice! The cabbage butterflies leave caterpillars that turn our kale and bok choi into swiss cheese and once in a while make it all the way onto your PLATE before you find them. And I know what you mean about the celery- I tried germinating them one year and nothing came up, so I bought starts, and by the end of the season the biggest stalks were the size of my pinkie finger. But wow was the flavor strong. It was great dehydrated for wintertime soup.
I think I see some dill seedlings in one of your pictures- I love that stuff because the black swallowtail butterflies lay eggs on them. I don't have the heart to hoe it down when it's feeding their caterpillars. If you poke them, their orange antennae pop out to scare you off, lol.

Pill bugs devouring your garden? That is just nuts! I wonder if it's a california thing or if your yard is an isopod perfect storm. I bet diatomaceous earth would nab them, but it would also nab every other thing with an exoskeleton that touched it, so maybe not great.
This is pretty fiddly and very small scale, but I hear you can use potato halves as traps for pill bugs. You cut the potato in half the long way and carve out a hollow in the flesh side of each piece. Then you nestle your bowl-shaped potatoes peel-side-up in your garden soil. The potato-cave will draw in pill bugs to eat the potato and use the cave as a humid shelter during the day, and each day you can pick it up and shake off the bugs into a plastic dish. Then you can toss them into your neighbor's yard, feed them to the toads under your yardlight, or give them to your kids to keep as pets. I'm not kidding either, I recently caught some to use to keep my tree frog's tank clean and they're an amusing piece of cake to care for. Mine are only brown or bluish, but I bet where you live you might find some orange or yellow-spotted ones!

My family grew a big garden this year even though we had wanted to downsize. A lot of the varieties we love have to be ordered from seed and then started indoors under lights, so I feel really lucky that that meant I had everything ordered by February. We grow too many things to bother listing, but one of my new favorites is the Round Mauve variety of eggplant. Love it, even the unidentified plant virus that popped up in our garden last year couldn't keep this eggplant down! And this year I grew the Blacktail Mountain watermelon for the first time. Along with the Crimson Sweet, it is now one of only two watermelons we can grow with any success in Nebraska. It takes up a weirdly small amount of space and the melons are tiny! But they actually get sweet, even in places with cool temps and a short season. We grew Amish cantaloupes which unexpectedly produced so well that we were struggling to find enough people to give them away to, until something discovered the patch and ate one or two whole melons every night! I think it was a deer based on the teeth marks. We also like Jimmy Nardello frying-peppers and some mildly hot ones like Pasilla Bajio, and Time Bomb and poblanos for stuffing.

posts.body_html:
My garden takes inspiration from the Native Americans. They would plant corn, beans, and squash together. The corn I grew this year was 'glass gem' popcorn. I took a course in the Native American/ early Spanish history in Florida and Georgia a while back. The professor said you could identify if a Native American site developed corn agriculture based on their tooth decay - so brush you teeth!




The squash is a Seminole Pumpkin. It has a thick rind and is one of the only varieties I've found to grow in the humid Southeast. Grows just as well in CA! The Spanish explorer Pánfilo de Narváez noted that the Apalachee grew these way back in 1528. Mike pointed out that these would grow up in trees so it must have been a sight to see! It's a shame they're not more common because they are so prolific and they're thick rind allows excellent storage. I still have one that's a year old. These five are leftovers from this year's crop after 4 pumpkin pies, a jack-o-lantern, giving a couple away, and a pumpkin thief stealing one!



Pumpkin flowers are edible and make a treat when pan fried. Male flowers are best.

The beans also did well and are easily dried for later, just not nearly as photogenic! I had no luck with root vegetables for the same pest reason - with the exception of ginger and horseradish. The moles certainly avoid those!

I'm trying a cultivated variety of purslane (Portulaca oleracea var. sativa) and Weywi Cupeli amaranth (Amaranthus cruentus) next growing season. I have to be careful with what greens I eat because oxalates cause kidney stones, but Amaranth greens have a safe level. Plus Amaranth grain is very nutritious.


Finally, I guess technically a vegetable is sugar cane. It's an old tradition in the southeast to boil the juice from the cane for syrup. The syrup has a distinct taste; kinda like a thinner molasses. It's mainly eaten with biscuits and sausage. My family's made syrup around Thanksgiving since at least my grandfather's grandparents. Here's a photo of the 80 gallon kettle in full boil a couple years ago. I'll miss it this year because of Covid, but some family members are having a social distancing version tomorrow. My family's cane patch in GA is right next to a swamp with U. radiata. Had to bring in carnivorous plants somewhere.



Even without access to a kettle in CA it is still nice to grow cane varieties that are over a century old. The stems can be eaten or used to sweeten a dish in cooking. Just as a side note, people in the Appalachians have a similar tradition with Sorghum.

Anything that's popcorn can be used as flour corn as well, and the variety I have is Dakota Black. Comparing images I can find, I'm not going to be convinced that Montana Morado is significantly darker than the darkest possible ears of Dakota, just has a different shape.

posts.body_html:
Great write-up Acalvin, thanks for sharing!

Okay, I'm officially OBSESSED with mostly asian greens right now. After sampling several varieties of some home grown, organically produced greens, holy Christ, they're so flavorful! It really turns you into a food A-hole: it's like upgrading from a boom box on your shoulder to having digital surround sound: you just can't go back to that boom box!
(for you youngsters, here's what a boom box is, I regret not carrying this around on my shoulder during my youth: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boombox )

I think the hardest thing about growing asian greens is figuring out when to plant them: everyone's climate and mico-climate is different, and this sometimes greatly affects their performance. Start them too early in the fall, and they'll bolt quickly with small plants if it's too hot. Start them in the summer, even if you're by the coast, and some will bolt because of the short nights. If it gets too cold in the winter, they'll bolt too! DANG MAN!

I guess you just have to get the right cultivars for your climate. I started all of my greens in september, and only one of them (the taiwanese loose leaf cabbage) is flowering before it could really size up.

Pics taken 12/2/20. This has been harvested multiple times already. The taiwanese loose leaf cabbage is in the background with the yellower leaves, it's crunchy, juicy, mild(not spicy) and even slightly sweet. High organic matter in the soil brings out the best flavors, don't rely solely on liquid or granular organic fertilizers, you won't get the same taste:



Here's the Gai Lan, or chinese broccoli. If you've been to an authentic chinese restraurant, they typically serve this steamed with oyster sauce. The stems are the best part. They're supposed to be harvested as soon as the first flowers open, otherwise the stems can get tough:


Here's Ellie holding some butter lettuce. OMG guys, you have to grow your own, it just tastes so much more amazing when it's picked and then immediately made into a salad:


And just so you can tell that I didn't go to the store and buy that stuff, haha:


Keep the pics and stories coming guys, would love to see what you're growing or have grown in your veggie garden!

purple broccoli. I was told by another grower decades ago, as long as you time them right and have the right variety, you can get decent sized heads. I tried sprouting these early in September, but they still turned out small. That said, they're way more flavorful than anything you can get at the store. Pics taken 1/8/20:


Chinese "loose leaf" lettuce. Great for salads, but even better for stir frying! I have a gut suspicion this is just romaine crossed with a close relative of Lactuca: it's slightly tougher than romaine once it warms up. Flavor is very unique, much richer, and seems more nutrient packed compared to western cultivars:


purple broccoli to the left, romanesco to the right. Yea, maybe they're just planted too close. I also might have under-done it with nitrogen: perhaps they should have gotten a little more earlier on to help the plants size up a bit:

posts.body_html:
Spent most of April planting some Chinese vegetables, but until they've grown out a little, what's in season right now is artichokes! A very easy perennial here in the SF Bay Area, I have three original plants grown from seeds about 4 years ago. These guys sprout up from the roots every year in the middle of our winter rains and don't need any extra irrigation to get decent artichokes once they're established. The flowers attract bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds if you leave a few buds on the plants to bloom. The seed heads are very prickly and have surprisingly few seeds in them, although we started getting volunteer seedlings this year. The plants die back through the hot summer and the dried stems are easy to pull by hand in the fall.


Our green artichoke. This one looks like the typical green globe artichokes you can get in a supermarket. The plant likes to sucker and has artichokes from mid-April through May.


This purple artichoke is my personal favorite. The plant doesn't sucker much at all and sets buds a few weeks before the green one. The texture after cooking is a little more solid and it tastes earthier than the green, which I really like. Once the artichoke flower buds start emerging, I blast them with water on occasion to keep the earwigs and aphids out. It's a little harder to clean the purple buds because the bracts can't be pulled apart with your bare hands - each bract has a prominent thorn unlike the green one.


These are tertiary artichokes, so they're about half the size of the primary and secondary ones, which have already been cut. I've seen artichoke plants get quite a bit taller than ours (more water? actual fertilizer?) but I like that these stay at a convenient height for harvesting and don't take up too much space.


The purple color was muted this year compared to last year's.


Artichokes are ready to cut once the bracts are slightly open; they're still edible later, but the size of the heart shrinks and everything's more fibrous. Leave a long stem on them - makes a good handle so you can dunk them underwater to get insects and dust out, and at this stage, the stem is as good as the heart. We don't do anything fancy with them: just snip off the ends of the bracts, steam for around 10 minutes (until a knife goes through the stem easily), and eat with a little mayonnaise or melted butter to cut the bitter notes.

All that said, these guys are super easy to grow around here (they are a thistle, after all!) - zero maintenance other than blasting the buds with water because earwigs will chew some meat off the bracts if you leave them alone, and removing old leaves and stems once they're dry. Some patience is required though since seedlings usually don't produce any buds the first year.

posts.body_html:
awesome Clue!!! Haven't tried artichokes since I was a kid: grew a fat plant, and before it produced, a gopher got the whole dang thing! Still bitter about that, LOL

Some more pics of the garden! for those of you who grow Broccoli and Cauliflower, let me know what varieties you've had success with. I've tried "D'Ciccio" twice now and both times (fall planting and spring planting) they've produced nice sized plants with 4-5 flowers, that's it! Remember, a regular sized broccoli inflorescence has hundreds or maybe in the low 1000's of flowers!!! They just can't take many days of heat or temperatures below 40F, that's what causes them to form those tiny heads. My neighbor grew belstar broccoli this year and he has 200 nice sized heads in his garden right now! Those went through two weeks of 90+F temps. this September/October with no ill effects!

That said, I tried growing Purple Cauliflower again (thought it was broccoli) and it produced smallish heads...but they were off the hook incredibly tasty! Never had cauliflower taste sweet like that before, it's probably from the cold nights:



These are the same celery seeds I grew last season, and they tasted absolutely amazing! This is Utah 52-70, seeds are now 20 years old and still very viable! Interestingly, I found some red variants in this seed batch, gonna cross this with the pink celery I got going:


here's the bed of celery, will take pics once they get bigger. Also sprinkled in some Calabrese broccoli in there, but they were started late, so I doubt they'll work:


Marvel of 4 seasons butter lettuce. OMG, butter lettuce is soooo good home grown, can't wait till these are ready:

awesome Clue!!!  Haven't tried artichokes since I was a kid: grew a fat plant, and before it produced, a gopher got the whole dang thing!  Still bitter about that, LOL
Some more pics of the garden!  for those of you who grow Broccoli and Cauliflower, let me know what varieties you've had success with. Remember, a regular sized broccoli inflorescence has hundreds or maybe in the low 1000's of flowers!!! posts.body_html:
did some trials on various purple broccoli varieties. Most of the pics in this post are from 3/27/22. Normally, at least in my climate, you're supposed to plant them end of July thru August, and then if you want to try a spring crop, you can start them indoors in February. Some purple broccoli require vernalization, or several weeks of very cold weather to produce heads. The newer varieties can produce normal sized heads and most don't require vernalization. I sowed most of the seeds in December 2021, which is actually not a good time to plant them, but they still worked!

What I'm starting to learn is that open pollinated seeds have high variability and low freqencies of high yielding individuals. There are a few winners in most of the batches though, so you can pheno hunt and improve them. On the other hand, the F1 hybrids are super productive, mostly uniform, and can produce decent sized heads.


Check out the size of the early purple sprouting broccoli plant. You're not supposed to give them much nitrogen, otherwise they grow large plants with very small heads. this was grown organically and given low Nitrogen, high P and high K. This is from open pollinated seeds:


Despite the enormous size of the plant, this is the main head, which is actually pretty big for this strain (early purple sprouting broccoli). These aren't bred for large heads, but rather a ton of small side shoots. There was so much variation in this seed batch, and a lot of the plants are less than exceptional. These seeds were 22 years old, they can last a very long time!


Here's the patch, with variable flowering times:


This was many weeks earlier, when they all got down to 24F, and the day after this pic was taken, it was 20F! Zero damage:


Now here's a new, selected (supposedly) F1 hybrid called Burgundy. These can actually produce regular sized heads, but thing is, I planted these the first week of January 2022, which is generally not recommended for broccoli in my climate. Nevertheless, it looks like they'll produce okay sized heads, they're still developing:




They're really beautiful plants. My neighbors see me staring at the plants for long periods of time, they probably think I'm slightly crazy:


Romanesco, from open pollinated seeds. I had great sized plants with great sized stems, but medium sized heads. will try some F1 hybrids this coming fall.

Had the most amazing winter veggie garden this season! Been eating salads every week for months now, and the only ones who are complaining are the kids of course! These pics were mostly taken in April 2022:

this is some overflow that I sent over to my neighbor!


purple passion Asparagus. This stuff is strange, it tastes like Aspargus, but definitely has sweetness to it! My patch doesn't produce much, but when it does produce, the spears are decent sized!




Here's Benny Goo-Goo holding purple of Sicily Cauliflower! Pretty amazing for open pollinated, which usually gives me poor results:


Ate Celery for breakfast for months! Great depth of flavor when grown at home organically. Hydrating, nutritious, and just makes you feel legit:


Benny being silly:


If you're going to try a purple broccoli variety, definitely give Burgundy a shot, it's the only one that actually forms decent sized heads and it tastes heavenly! The stems are crazy sweet:


Here's burgundy "in Plantu" which is MW's made up way of saying "on the plant"



Here's Shy Ellie Boo-Boo posing for a pic:



I trialed many different F1 hybrid diakon radishes specifically meant for spring planting, and all of them bolted/produced nothing except Fujizuke(sp?). My wife saw this and said she's gonna make some turnip cakes, YESSSSSSSSSSSSSSS!!!!!!


green magic F1, didn't button despite temperatures below 40F and temps above 80F during development:

posts.body_html:
Hard to tell the size of these heads, but they're big enough that a family of 4 can't finish it in one sitting! I'm no longer EVER going to grow those crappy open pollinated green broccoli varieties (eg. Calabrese, de Ciccio, Waltham 29, etc). This is the reason that I've failed with Broccoli my whole life until now! In fact, I have no clue how ANYONE EVER has success with those varieties unless they live in the absolute perfect climate! If there's more than 3 days of temperatures below 40F or 3 days above 78F during the plant's development, they will button and produce no more than a bite to eat, even on large plants! This happened to me over and over again, and I always thought I was doing something wrong, but turns out everything was done right, except the variety!

In contrast, the F1 broccoli hybrids I grew went through several light frosts, countless days of night temperatures below 40F, and a few days above 80 while in vegetative growth and they ALL still produced decent sized heads! I grew packman, emerald jewel, lieutenant, green magic, and Burney (all F1 hybrids). The only one to show any stress or damage from the frost was Packman, but that variety looks like it'll produce the biggest heads, and it takes the longest to mature.

Here's Lieutenant, started second week of February and harvested end of May! This F1 hybrid is a new select cultivar bred to withstand heat, and from my experience, it can also take the cold! It can be successfully grown even in the deep south, provided it's planted at the right time.



Here's emerald jewel, another F1 hybrid that is a great performer and also a looker!


This is green magic F1, the fastest to produce. It also produces an abundance of side shoots once you harvest the main head, so you definitely get a lot of mileage per plant!


We've been eating organic broccoli for weeks now and it's way worth the effort! The stems are sweet and when grown organically with lots of compost in the soil, they have a depth of flavor you can't get at the grocery store!
